subject: Identifying all indirect paths in a model

messages.author: bc810b1d0900407f
messages.subject: Identifying all indirect paths in a model
parts:
Dear All,

I vaguely recall there is a discussion a while ago on identifying indirect paths in a lavaan model, similar to what AMOS does. I am working on all_indirect_paths() (https://sfcheung.github.io/manymome/reference/all_indirect_paths.html), a function for a package by a friend and I (manymome, https://cran.r-project.org/package=manymome), that gets the output of lavaan() or its wrappers (i.e., a lavaan-class object) and enumerates all indirect paths (a path with at least one mediator). I found that this task can already be done with the help of using all_simple_paths() from the igraph package:

https://igraph.org/r/doc/all_simple_paths.html

Maybe others are also interested in this approach and so I share it here.

This is an illustration:

library(igraph)
library(lavaan)
mod <-
"
m11 ~ x1 + x2
m12 ~ m11 + x1 + x2
m2 ~ x1 + x2
y1 ~ m2 + m12 + m11 + x1 + x2
y2 ~ m2 + m12 + m11 + x1 + x2
"
fit0 <- sem(mod, do.fit = FALSE, fixed.x = FALSE)

# The beta matrix

tmp <- lavInspect(fit0)$beta
tmp
#> m11 m12 m2 y1 y2 x1 x2
#> m11 0 0 0 0 0 1 2
#> m12 3 0 0 0 0 4 5
#> m2 0 0 0 0 0 6 7
#> y1 10 9 8 0 0 11 12
#> y2 15 14 13 0 0 16 17
#> x1 0 0 0 0 0 0 0
#> x2 0 0 0 0 0 0 0

# Covnert the beta matrix to an adjacency matrix

tmp[tmp > 0] <- 1
# We need to transpose it before passing to graph_from_adjacency_matrix()
tmp <- t(tmp)
tmp
#> m11 m12 m2 y1 y2 x1 x2
#> m11 0 1 0 1 1 0 0
#> m12 0 0 0 1 1 0 0
#> m2 0 0 0 1 1 0 0
#> y1 0 0 0 0 0 0 0
#> y2 0 0 0 0 0 0 0
#> x1 1 1 1 1 1 0 0
#> x2 1 1 1 1 1 0 0

# Create an igraph object from the adjaceny matrix

gtmp <- graph_from_adjacency_matrix(tmp, mode = "directed")
plot(gtmp)

# Find all paths from x1 to y1 using all_simple_paths()

x1_to_y1 <- all_simple_paths(gtmp, from = "x1", to = "y1")

# The output is a list of igraph.vs objects. Their names store the names of the nodes (variables)
# The names can be extracted by lapply() and names()

out <- lapply(x1_to_y1, names)
out
#> [[1]]
#> [1] "x1" "m11" "m12" "y1"
#>
#> [[2]]
#> [1] "x1" "m11" "y1"
#>
#> [[3]]
#> [1] "x1" "m12" "y1"
#>
#> [[4]]
#> [1] "x1" "m2" "y1"
#>
#> [[5]]
#> [1] "x1" "y1"

By removing paths with only two elements, (e.g., x1 -> y1), this method can be used to enumerate all indirect paths in a model.

This method works for typical path models with observed variables:

https://sfcheung.github.io/manymome/articles/med_lm.html#identifying-all-indirect-paths

The vignette above is for model parameters estimated by lm() but it can also work for a model fitted by lavaan, as in the following example for a model with latent variables:

https://sfcheung.github.io/manymome/articles/med_lav.html#identifying-all-indirect-paths

I do not use the output to generate model syntax and define indirect effects because we use an approach that probably is uncommon in lavaan for computing indirect effects and forming their CIs. In manymome, we extract parameters directly so that users do not need to label any parameters in the model syntax to compute indirect effects. Therefore, just the variable names (latent or observed) are enough for us.

Nevertheless, this approach can also be modified for tools that generate or modify model syntax, e.g., by adding labels to the parameters and then adding the definitions of user parameters by ":=" using these labels. Therefore, I share it here so that interested members may implement it in ways suitable for their functions or packages.

Comments and suggestions on using all_simple_paths() this way, e.g., problems and pitfalls, are welcome.

-- Shu Fai

P.S.: all_indirect_paths() is not yet in the CRAN version of manymome.

messages.author: ff3a366aa7a9b488
messages.subject: Re: Identifying all indirect paths in a model
parts:
Hi Shu, 

This is great. Thanks a lot for your work. I posted a script on the forum some time ago that tries to find and bootstrap all indirect paths. But the solution is very computationally intensive and not suitable for models with many LV. Additionally, I never put the tool to a serious test: https://groups.google.com/g/lavaan/c/0RSsh4M6zQg/m/V2zKKV7FAwAJ (Third or fourth post). Your solution seems to be much less computationally intensive - fantastic. 

 Best

Christian
